title: learnèd sisters
short: The nine Muses, daughters of Zeus and Memory, invoked in the conventional opening of a classical marriage hymn.
body: The 'learned sisters' are the Muses. Spenser reminds them that they have helped him praise others (the great patrons of his earlier poems) and have also mourned their 'owne mishaps', which editors take as a glance at his Teares of the Muses (1591), where each Muse laments the neglect of learning, and at his elegies and 'complaints'. The opening stanza therefore surveys Spenser's own career, moving from public praise and lament to a private subject: 'mine owne loves prayses'. The invocation follows the epithalamic convention of calling the singer's helpers to the wedding, but it is unusually personal, because the poet will be his own bridegroom.

title: Orpheus and his bride
short: Orpheus, the archetypal poet, sang for his bride Eurydice; the precedent licenses a poet's singing at his own wedding.
body: Orpheus, son of the Muse Calliope, is the model of the poet whose song moves woods, rocks and beasts, which prepares the refrain's answering woods. The precedent is double-edged. In Ovid's account the wedding of Orpheus and Eurydice was ill-omened: Hymen came, but his torch only sputtered and smoked, and the bride soon died of a snakebite (Metamorphoses 10.1-10). Critics have observed that Spenser's choice of Orpheus introduces, from the first stanza, the shadow of loss and the fragility of time that the poem's numerical and seasonal design tries to master. The allusion also anticipates the poem's own torch-bearing Hymen in the next stanza.

title: The occasion: the poet's own wedding
short: Spenser sings his own marriage to Elizabeth Boyle, celebrated in Ireland on 11 June 1594 and printed with the Amoretti in 1595.
body: An epithalamium was normally written by a poet for someone else's wedding, as Catullus did for Manlius Torquatus (Carmen 61). Spenser's innovation is to be both singer and groom. He married Elizabeth Boyle, a kinswoman of Richard Boyle (later Earl of Cork), on 11 June 1594 (the usual date, inferred largely from the poem's own reference to St Barnabas's Day), probably in or near Cork; a local tradition places the ceremony in Cork, but this is not documented. The poem was published by William Ponsonby in 1595 in a single volume, Amoretti and Epithalamion, so that the sonnet sequence of courtship leads into the marriage song. 'Alone' stresses the self-sufficiency of the poet's voice, answered only by woods and echo.

title: The refrain
short: Each stanza ends with a varied refrain on woods answering and echo ringing; it turns negative once night falls.
body: The long final line of every stanza, an alexandrine, is a refrain modelled on the refrains of classical wedding songs (Catullus's repeated cry to Hymen) and on the Italian canzone, whose stanza form Spenser adapts. The refrain is never quite identical: pronouns shift ('me', 'you', 'theyr'), the verb moves from future to present, and after the bride is put to bed it becomes negative ('The woods no more shall answere, nor your echo ring', l. 314). Readers have treated these modulations as a clock: the public noise of the day gives way to the silence and privacy of night. Echo, the nymph who can only repeat, makes the natural world a chorus to the poet's single voice.

title: Hymen ... his bright Tead
short: Hymen, god of marriage, leads the wedding procession ('maske') with a torch whose sparks are its 'flakes'.
body: Hymen (Hymenaeus) is the classical god of marriage, whose name was shouted in the wedding procession. His 'maske' is a masque or ceremonial procession, the pageant that escorted the bride. 'Tead' is a Spenserian borrowing of Latin taeda, the pine torch carried before the bride in Roman weddings and one of Hymen's standard attributes; 'flake' here means a spark or flash of flame. Catullus calls on Hymen to shake the pine torch (Carmen 61), which is the likely model. The 'bachelors' in fresh garments are the groom's young male attendants, matched later by the 'damzels' of the bride.

title: usury of long delight
short: The wedding day pays the bride interest on the 'paynes and sorrowes' of courtship, a financial conceit for long-delayed joy.
body: Usury is interest on a loan. The image treats the pains of the long courtship recorded in the Amoretti as a debt or investment that the wedding will repay with interest in the form of lasting delight. The conceit is daring, since usury was morally suspect in Spenser's England (the 1571 statute allowed it only within limits), but here it is harmless and joyful. The same accounting language returns at nightfall, when night 'defrays' the day's labour and 'sums' and 'cancels' the lover's cares (ll. 316-18), so the poem frames love as a ledger finally settled.

title: turtle dove
short: The turtle-dove, emblem of faithful married love; the aubade calling the beloved to rise also echoes the Song of Songs.
body: The turtle-dove was proverbial for constancy, since it was believed to take only one mate. Spenser's call to wake the bride recalls the Song of Songs 2:10-14: 'Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away ... the voice of the turtle is heard in our land ... O my dove'. Editors have long noted that the poem blends this biblical aubade with classical epithalamic convention, so that Christian and pagan sources of marriage poetry run together throughout. The Canticles' imagery recurs more strongly in the blazon of stanza 10.

title: Mulla
short: Mulla is Spenser's name for the river Awbeg near his Kilcolman estate in County Cork; the stanza localises the classical nymphs in Ireland.
body: Spenser lived at Kilcolman Castle, near Doneraile in north Cork, on land granted to him in the Munster plantation. In Colin Clouts Come Home Againe and The Faerie Queene (IV.xi.41) he calls the local river Awbeg 'Mulla' and mythologises it. Here the classical nymphs of river, lake and mountain are given Irish homes: Mulla's trout and pike, the 'rushy lake' (usually taken as the marshy lough by Kilcolman), and the hills where deer are hunted. Critics working on Spenser in Ireland note that the stanza turns contested colonial land into a pastoral landscape that serves the English poet's wedding.

title: The Rosy Morne ... Tithones bed
short: Dawn (Aurora) rises from the bed of her mortal husband Tithonus, a formula from Homer and Virgil.
body: Aurora, the Dawn, was married to the Trojan prince Tithonus, for whom she won immortality but not eternal youth. The epic formula of Dawn leaving Tithonus's bed opens Odyssey 5 and is imitated by Virgil ('Tithoni croceum linquens Aurora cubile', Aeneid 4.585). 'Rosy Morne' renders Homer's 'rosy-fingered' Dawn. Spenser borrows epic grandeur for the hour of the bride's waking; the myth's undertone of a love that endures while the mortal partner ages suits a poem preoccupied with time. Phoebus (the sun) follows in the next line.

title: Larke ... Mavis ... Ouzell ... Ruddock
short: A dawn chorus: lark, thrush, mavis (song-thrush), ouzel (blackbird) and ruddock (robin) sing in harmonised parts.
body: The birds form a choir singing the 'mattins' (morning office) of the church of love. 'Mavis' is a dialect name for the song-thrush and 'Ouzell' for the blackbird; 'Ruddock' is the robin. Since thrush and mavis may be the same bird, editors suggest Spenser means two kinds of thrush (the mistle-thrush and song-thrush) or simply enjoys the list. The vocabulary is musical: a 'descant' is a melody sung above a plainsong, and 'consent' means harmony (Latin concentus) as well as agreement. The bird chorus was a commonplace of the medieval reverdie and of wedding poetry.

title: ye fayre houres
short: The Hours (Horae), goddesses of the seasons, here children of Day and Night, dress the bride; Hieatt's reading makes them the poem's structure.
body: In Hesiod the Horae are daughters of Zeus and Themis (Theogony 901-3) and guardians of the seasons. Spenser instead makes them children of Jove's paradise 'of Day and Night', a genealogy that suits a poem about one day and one night. The Hours were attendants of Venus as well as keepers of time, so here they join the Graces in adorning the bride. A. Kent Hieatt argued that the hours are the hidden structural key: the poem's 24 stanzas correspond to the hours of the wedding day and night. Not all critics accept his full scheme, but the hours' presence at this point is generally read as self-referential.

anchor: three handmayds of the Cyprian Queene
title: three handmayds of the Cyprian Queene
short: The three Graces, attendants of Venus (the 'Cyprian Queen', worshipped on Cyprus), adorn the bride and 'throw between' graces.
body: Venus was born from the sea near Cyprus and was worshipped at Paphos; hence 'Cyprian Queene'. The three Graces (Euphrosyne, Aglaia, Thalia in Hesiod's naming) were her handmaids. Spenser gave them a major visionary role in The Faerie Queene VI.x, where Colin Clout pipes to them on Mount Acidale and a fourth grace, usually identified with Colin's own beloved, stands in their midst; many critics connect that scene with Elizabeth Boyle. The pun in 'Some graces to be seene' (graceful touches, and the goddesses themselves) is typical of Spenser's wordplay.

title: pipe ... tabor ... Croud ... tymbrels
short: A rustic band: pipe, small drum, 'crowd' (a fiddle, from Welsh crwth) and the girls' tambourines ('tymbrels').
body: The minstrels play popular instruments: the pipe and tabor (a small drum played by the same performer) and the 'croud' or crowd, a bowed stringed instrument, from Welsh crwth, often used loosely for a fiddle. 'Trembling' describes its vibrating tone. The 'tymbrels' are tambourines; the word recalls Miriam and the women of Israel dancing with timbrels in Exodus 15:20. 'Withouten breach or jar' carries a moral as well as musical sense: harmony among instruments mirrors social and marital concord.

title: Hymen, iö Hymen
short: The ritual shout of the Roman wedding procession, taken from Catullus's 'io Hymen Hymenaee'.
body: Roman wedding processions escorted the bride to her husband's house with the cry 'io Hymen Hymenaee', which serves as the refrain of Catullus 61 and 62. The diaeresis in 'iö' marks two syllables. Spenser transfers the cry to the boys of an Irish town running through the street, and the crowd 'applauds' as if at a theatre. The scene emphasises the public, communal phase of the day, which later gives way to the hushed private night; James Lambert and others have described this as the poem's movement from communal ritual to private affect.

title: Arysing forth to run her mighty race
short: Echoes Psalm 19:5, where the sun comes forth 'as a bridegroom' and 'as a strong man to run a race', here transferred to the bride.
body: Psalm 19:4-5 describes the sun, 'which is as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, and rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race'. Spenser reverses the genders and the planet: the bride, compared to the moon goddess, comes from 'her chamber of the East' to run her race. The allusion gives the procession a cosmic and scriptural dignity and links the bride to the heavenly bodies that measure time, one of the poem's controlling concerns. It is one of several places where the poem joins classical deities with the language of the Psalms.

title: ye merchants daughters
short: The poet turns to the townswomen as audience: the wedding takes place in a provincial town, among its merchant families.
body: After invoking nymphs and goddesses, the poet appeals to the merchants' daughters of the 'towne', usually taken to be Cork or Youghal, the ports near the Boyle family. The shift of audience is striking: the bride's beauty is displayed before ordinary townswomen as well as before the deities of the earlier stanzas. Critics have read the line as a mark of the poem's social realism and of the Anglo-Irish urban setting of the marriage. The question 'did ye see / So fayre a creature' introduces the formal catalogue of the bride's beauty, the blazon.

title: The blazon
short: A head-to-breast catalogue of the bride's beauties in the manner of the Song of Songs; 'uncrudded' means uncurdled.
body: Stanza 10 is a blazon, the Petrarchan inventory of a woman's features, but its homely comparisons (apples, cherries, a bowl of cream, budding lilies) recall the Song of Songs, whose bride has a neck 'like the tower of David' (4:4) and 'as a tower of ivory' (7:4); compare 'snowie necke lyke to a marble towre'. 'Uncrudded' means not curdled, smooth and fresh; 'rudded' means reddened. Readers disagree over the effect: some find the domestic images charmingly rustic, others see a deliberately sensuous catalogue that the next stanza corrects by praising the 'inward beauty' no eye can see.

title: like a palace fair
short: The body as a palace climbing by stairs to the 'seat' of honour and the 'bower' of chastity, an allegory of the soul's dwelling.
body: The image of the body as a building governed from its upper storeys is ancient (Plato's tripartite soul, with reason in the head) and is developed at length in Spenser's House of Alma in The Faerie Queene II.ix. Here the ascent ends in 'honors seat and chastities sweet bowre', the head and the mind where virtue rules. The figure turns the blazon's physical catalogue toward moral meaning and prepares for the next stanza, in which virtue reigns 'as Queene in royal throne' over the 'base affections'.

title: Medusaes mazeful hed
short: Seeing her inner beauty would astonish like Medusa's head, which turned beholders to stone; 'red' means saw, beheld.
body: Medusa, the Gorgon slain by Perseus, turned to stone whoever looked at her (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4-5). 'Red' is a past tense of 'read' in the old sense of perceive or look upon; 'mazeful' means bewildering, amazing. The comparison is bold, since Medusa is monstrous, but its point is the stunning, petrifying power of a sight beyond ordinary sight. The stanza's 'inward beauty' and 'heavenly guifts' reflect the Neoplatonic doctrine, developed in Spenser's Fowre Hymnes, that true beauty is of the soul, while the 'base affections' obeying virtue echo the moral psychology of the House of Alma.

title: Open the temple gates
short: Echoes Psalm 24:7, 'Lift up your heads, O ye gates', as the procession reaches the church and the poem turns to Christian rite.
body: The command to open the gates and deck the posts recalls both Psalm 24:7-9 ('Lift up your heads, O ye gates ... and the King of glory shall come in') and the Roman custom of adorning the doorposts of the bridegroom's house. The 'temple' is the parish church; the bride is called a 'Saynt', and the ceremony that makes 'endlesse matrimony' is the Protestant marriage service of the Book of Common Prayer, with organ and anthem. Critics have treated stanzas 12-13 as the sacred centre of the poem, where classical festivity gives way to Christian sacrament without either being rejected.

title: dyde in grayne
short: Her blush is like crimson dyed 'in grain', that is, with fast colour from kermes ('grain'), so deep it cannot wash out.
body: 'Grain' was the name for kermes, the dried insects that yielded scarlet dye, and to dye 'in grain' was to dye fast and thoroughly. The blush spreading over the 'pure snow' of the bride's face is thus permanent in colour though momentary in occurrence, a characteristic Spenserian paradox. The red-and-white complexion is a Petrarchan commonplace, but the setting before the altar makes it a sign of modesty under the priest's blessing. The angels who forget their service to peep at her face are a daring, half-playful touch that critics have often admired.

title: sad eyes
short: 'Sad' here means grave, serious and steadfast, not sorrowful.
body: In Elizabethan English 'sad' often meant serious, sober or steadfast (from Old English sæd, sated, then firm); the sense of sorrowful was only one of its meanings. The bride's eyes are fixed on the ground in modesty and governed so that no glance strays 'awry' to admit 'a little thought unsownd' (unsound, improper). Her hand given to the groom is 'the pledge of all our band', the band (bond) of marriage, joined in the service's handfasting. The stanza ends with the angels singing Alleluia, the climax of the sacred action.

anchor: sprinkle all the postes and wals
title: Bacchus and the feast
short: The feast returns to classical revelry: wine poured freely, posts sprinkled, Bacchus and Hymen crowned, the Graces dancing.
body: After the church service the poem resumes classical festivity. Pouring wine 'by the belly full' and sprinkling the posts and walls recall ancient wedding and festival customs; the walls that 'sweat' and become 'drunken' are a comic hyperbole. Bacchus, god of wine, is crowned with a 'coronall' (garland), and Hymen with vine leaves. Critics differ on how far this licence is controlled: some see a happy coexistence of pagan joy and Christian sacrament, others a deliberate contrast that the following stanzas, with their anxiety about time, temper.

title: Barnaby the bright
short: St Barnabas's Day, 11 June, which under the Julian calendar fell at the summer solstice: the longest day and shortest night.
body: Spenser's wedding took place on St Barnabas's Day, 11 June 1594. In the Julian calendar, still used in England, the date coincided with the summer solstice, hence the proverb 'Barnaby bright, the longest day and the shortest night'. After the solstice the sun begins to decline once it 'sees the Crab behind his back', that is, once it has entered the zodiacal sign of Cancer. The poet complains comically that he has chosen the longest day, when a long night would have suited him better. Hieatt's numerical reading depends on this date: the poem's proportion of day to night stanzas matches the hours of daylight at the solstice in southern Ireland.

title: Stanza 15: the short stanza
short: This stanza alone has seventeen lines, lacking the usual short line; scholars debate whether the irregularity is meaningful.
body: Most stanzas of the poem have eighteen or nineteen lines, with short trimeter lines placed at regular intervals. The bell-ringing stanza has only seventeen, because it omits the expected short line after its ninth line, though its rhyme scheme is complete. Explanations range from authorial slip to number symbolism. John Hale and Stefan Lane weigh the possibilities without settling the matter: a slip or printing error seems unlikely given the complete rhyme scheme, numerology explains little, and they find the idea that the missing short line enacts the complaint about the long day and short night rather obvious. They also consider that the irregular rhythm might imitate the jangling of the bells the stanza addresses.

title: the bright evening-star ... out of the East
short: The evening star cannot rise in the east at sunset; editors debate whether this is a slip or an intended paradox.
body: The evening star is Hesperus, the planet Venus seen after sunset, and it always appears in the western sky, near where the sun has set. Spenser's 'out of the East' is therefore astronomically impossible. Some editors take it as a slip or a loose use of a conventional phrase; others propose symbolic readings, for instance that the star rises like the bride (who earlier came 'from her chamber of the East') or that Venus as both morning and evening star joins dawn and dusk. The Variorum commentary records the problem. Spenser earlier compared the bride's eyes to Hesperus (l. 95), and the star is addressed here as Venus's 'lampe of love'.

title: Maia ... Tempe ... the Acidalian brooke
short: The bride in bed is compared to Maia lying in Tempe after bathing in the Acidalian spring, haunt of the Graces.
body: Maia, eldest of the Pleiades, bore Mercury (Hermes) to Jove. Tempe is the beautiful valley of the river Peneus in Thessaly. The Acidalian spring, associated in ancient commentary with Venus and the Graces, gives its name to Mount Acidale in The Faerie Queene VI.x, where Colin Clout sees the Graces dance. No classical source tells this particular story of Maia, and editors regard the scene as Spenser's own combination of mythic places. The comparison eroticises the bride while keeping her in a landscape of innocence and grace, 'Twixt sleepe and wake'.

title: Now welcome, night!
short: The turn to night: the refrain falls silent, and night is asked to cover the lovers and settle the account of the day's cares.
body: Stanza 17 puts the bride to bed ('Now it is night'), and stanza 18 welcomes night itself, so the poem passes from public day to private night. Night is welcomed in the financial language seen earlier: it 'defrays' the long day's labour and has 'sumd' and 'cancellèd' the lover's cares. The bride's attendants have been dismissed, and the refrain now commands the woods and echo to be silent. Hieatt noted that night falls at the point corresponding to the number of daylight hours on the wedding day; whether or not one accepts his calculation, the shift in the refrain makes the change audible.

title: Alcmena ... the great Tirynthian groome ... Majesty
short: Jove lengthened the night when he begot Hercules (of Tiryns) on Alcmena; Spenser also has Night bear Majesty to Jove.
body: Jove, disguised as Amphitryon, lay with Alcmena and prolonged the night to enjoy her, begetting Hercules, called 'Tirynthian' from Tiryns, the city of his foster-father (the story is told in Plautus's Amphitruo and elsewhere). 'Groome' here means young man or hero. The second myth, that Jove lay with Night and 'begot Majesty', has no clear classical source: in Ovid's Fasti (5.11-52) Majesty is the child of Honour and Reverence. Editors therefore treat it as Spenser's invention, apt for a poem that hopes the marriage night will produce noble offspring.

title: the Pouke ... hob Goblins
short: A charm against night terrors: Puck (the 'pouke'), hobgoblins, witches, owls and ravens are banished from the bridal house.
body: The 'Pouke' is the puck or pooka, a mischievous or malign spirit of English and Irish folklore (Irish púca), later domesticated by Shakespeare's Robin Goodfellow in A Midsummer Night's Dream. 'Hob Goblins' are household goblins; Spenser adds the sceptical aside 'names whose sence we see not'. The stanza is an apotropaic catalogue, a formal warding-off of evil, in which owls, the night raven and croaking frogs are omens of death. Such charms belong to the epithalamic tradition, which often prays that no ill omen will disturb the couple; the Irish setting gives the folklore a local colour.

title: Cinthia ... the Latmian shepherd
short: The moon (Cynthia), lover of Endymion, the shepherd of Mount Latmos, is asked to bless the marriage as goddess of childbirth.
body: Cynthia (Diana, from Mount Cynthus on Delos) is the moon. Her love for Endymion, the shepherd of Mount Latmos, was a favourite Elizabethan story. Spenser's detail of 'a fleece of wooll' comes from Virgil's Georgics 3.391-3, where the god Pan wins the Moon with a gift of snowy wool; Spenser transfers the gift to Endymion. As Lucina, the moon goddess presided over childbirth ('wemens labours'), so she is asked to 'informe' (give form to) the womb with seed. The prayers for children in the closing stanzas reflect the Prayer Book's first purpose of marriage, the procreation of children.

title: Juno ... Genius ... Hebe
short: Juno, patroness of marriage and childbirth; Genius, god of generation and the 'geniall' marriage bed; Hebe, goddess of youth.
body: Juno was the Roman goddess of marriage (Juno Pronuba) and of childbirth (Juno Lucina), hence called on 'of women in their smart'. Genius was the guardian spirit of procreation; the marriage bed was the lectus genialis, so 'geniall bed' plays on the Latin. Spenser's Genius also appears at the gate of the Garden of Adonis (Faerie Queene III.vi.31-3), the mythic seedbed of all generation. Hebe, daughter of Juno, is goddess of youth. The poem thus moves through a ladder of powers, from the moon to Juno to the gods of heaven, each asked for fruitful offspring.

title: heavenly tabernacles
short: The final prayer extends from children to their salvation: descendants who will rise to heaven and swell the number of saints.
body: The last stanza addresses the heavens as a temple lit by the stars' 'thousand torches' and prays for a 'large posterity' who will possess the earth and then 'inherit' heavenly dwellings. 'Tabernacles' is biblical (compare 'everlasting habitations', Luke 16:9, and the earthly 'tabernacle' of 2 Corinthians 5:1); 'influence' is the astrological flowing of stellar power. The prayer ties the one day of the wedding to the end of time, completing the poem's movement from hours to years to eternity, and to the Protestant ideal of marriage as producing godly heirs.

title: The envoy
short: A seven-line envoy, like a canzone's tornata, offers the song as the bride's wedding gift; its 'hasty accidents' are much debated.
body: The envoy, in the manner of the Italian canzone's closing stanza, addresses the poem itself. It is to replace 'many ornaments' with which the bride should have been adorned but which, 'through hasty accidents', were cut off. What these accidents were is unknown. Suggestions include ornaments or gifts that failed to arrive in time, a hurried wedding, or a poem (or another work) that Spenser had meant to finish for the occasion; 'Ye would not stay your dew time to expect' is taken by some to address the occasion itself, by others the ornaments. The syntax is notoriously knotted, and editors print different punctuation.

title: for short time an endlesse moniment
short: The last line sums up the poem's design: a single short day made a lasting monument, built from hours and days in number.
body: The poem has 24 stanzas (23 with the refrain plus the closing envoy) and 365 long lines, which A. Kent Hieatt (1960) read as the hours of the day and the days of the year, so that one day of marriage stands for the year's cycle and, through it, for time made eternal. Hieatt's further claims, such as the pairing of stanzas across the two halves and the arrival of night at the seventeenth stanza (matching the daylight hours of a southern Irish midsummer), have been more contested, but the basic counts are accepted. The final phrase also echoes the classical boast that poetry outlasts bronze (Horace, Odes 3.30, 'exegi monumentum'): the short time of one wedding becomes endless in verse.
